summary: This bill prohibits U.S. courts from enforcing judgments, contracts, or arbitration decisions based on Shari’a or other foreign law if doing so would violate any party's constitutional rights.

scores.thoughts: The bill contains no provisions related to federal, state, or local government expenditures, appropriations, or budgetary matters. It is exclusively focused on judicial application of law.
No references to tax policy, rates, deductions, or revenue collection appear in the bill text.
The legislation does not address healthcare systems, insurance, public coverage, or market-based reforms.
No content pertains to firearms regulation, Second Amendment enforcement, or gun rights protections.
The bill makes no changes to immigration law, border policy, visas, or pathways to citizenship.
There are no provisions concerning reproductive rights, abortion access, or restrictions.
The text does not mention military funding, defense policy, or armed forces appropriations.
No environmental regulations, climate policy, or conservation measures are addressed.
The bill contains nothing related to welfare programs, food assistance, or entitlement reforms.
No sections deal with schools, federal education funding, school choice, or curriculum policy.
The legislation does not engage with drug enforcement, decriminalization, or controlled substances.
While the bill addresses court procedures, it focuses solely on choice of law in civil/family matters and does not alter criminal sentencing, policing, or rehabilitation policies.
No provisions relate to tariffs, trade agreements, or protectionism.
The bill has no fiscal implications or statements regarding deficits or debt reduction.
The legislation does not address legal protections or restrictions specific to LGBTQ+ individuals.
No content concerns foreign assistance programs or international aid funding.
The bill does not touch on voting rights, election administration, or voter ID requirements.
There are no references to technology regulation, data privacy, or digital oversight.
The text does not engage with union rights, worker protections, or employer flexibility.

The bill affirms individuals' freedom to practice religion voluntarily but prohibits courts from enforcing foreign or religious law (specifically Shari’a) that conflicts with constitutional rights. This is a narrow procedural rule on choice of law rather than a broad policy on religious exemptions versus civil rights enforcement.
